hints.text: Add the two fractions over the common denominator $\sin\theta(1 + \cos\theta)$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up on $\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} + \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}$: over the common denominator $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ the numerator becomes $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$. Combine first, then let the identity collapse the top.
That is $2 + 2\cos\theta = 2(1 + \cos\theta)$, so the fraction reduces to $\frac{2}{\sin\theta} = 2\csc\theta$.

explanation: Use the common denominator $\sin\theta(1 + \cos\theta)$; the numerator becomes $\sin^2\theta + (1 + \cos\theta)^2$.
Now the $(1 + \cos\theta)$ cancels top and bottom, leaving $\frac{2}{\sin\theta}$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Sanity-check at $\theta = 90^\circ$
steps: Now test $\theta = 30^\circ$: the expression gives about $4$, and $2\csc 30^\circ = 4$ ✓ — choice B would have been stuck at $2$ forever.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap is answering $2$ (choice B), by noticing the two fractions look like reciprocals of each other and assuming they add to $2$.
Reciprocals multiply to $1$; they do not add to $2$ unless each one happens to equal $1$.

One test angle exposes it instantly: at $\theta = 30^\circ$ the expression equals $4$, not $2$. When an identity "feels" true, plug in an angle other than $90^\circ$ before you trust it. The answer is $2\csc\theta$.
